metric_rationale: The metric computes the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the prediction of Take The Best (TTB). Because the experimental design pits TTB and Tallying directly against each other on most trials (where TTB has a strong preference for one option and Tallying has a strong preference for the other), TTB simulated subjects will score very close to 1.0, whereas Tallying simulated subjects will score close to 0.125 (since they choose the opposite of TTB on 6 out of 8 trial types, and guess on the remaining 2). This creates an extremely large and stable gap between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that are consistent with the Tallying heuristic on trials where Tallying predicts a strict preference (i.e., excluding ties). Given the experimental design, the trials where Tallying has a strict preference are precisely those where Take The Best (TTB) makes the opposite prediction. Therefore, data generated by the Tallying model will yield a metric value close to 1.0, whereas data generated by TTB will yield a value close to 0.0. This maximal divergence guarantees strong discrimination between the two theories.

The metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. Because the experiment is designed with many 'conflict' trials where TTB and Weighted Additive (WADD) models predict opposite choices, this match rate will be high for data generated by TTB and low for data generated by WADD.

In this specific experimental design, Take The Best (TTB) will consistently choose Option A across all 8 trial types because Option A is always favored by the highest-validity discriminating cue. Weighted Additive (WADD), however, compensates for the highest-validity cue by summing the weights of multiple lower-validity cues, leading it to choose Option B on several trial types (e.g., Trial 1, where the four lower cues easily outweigh the top cue even at high gamma). The mean of the 'response' column (proportion of Option B choices) will therefore be near 0 for TTB (driven only by noise/lapses) and significantly higher for WADD.

Probabilistic Take The Best (Prob TTB) models cue search via a Plackett-Luce process. However, because its gamma parameter is uniformly sampled up to 100, about 80% of Prob TTB subjects behave almost deterministically, ignoring lower-validity cues. This causes metrics based on the population mean to fail, as the large majority of subjects show no difference between the two theories. However, the ~20% of Prob TTB subjects with a low gamma parameter will exhibit a strong positive correlation between the number of opposing cues favoring Option B and their likelihood of choosing Option B. Deterministic TTB, on the other hand, predicts a correlation of exactly zero (in expectation) for all subjects, regardless of noise levels. To isolate this distinct sub-population, this metric computes the subject-level Pearson correlation and returns the 90th percentile across the pooled sample. This non-linear aggregation captures the heavy right tail of the Prob TTB distribution, producing a massive point estimate gap, while maintaining the tight between-subject variance of the raw correlations.

By partitioning trials into those where the TTB-favored option faces exactly 1 opposing cue (Trials 1, 5, 7) versus 3 or more opposing cues (Trials 3, 4, 6), we create a sharp contrast between the two models. Deterministic TTB bases its decision solely on the single best cue, making it entirely blind to the number of opposing cues; thus, it predicts an expected difference of exactly 0 between these two trial sets. Probabilistic TTB samples cues proportionally to their exponentiated validities, meaning that encountering 3+ opposing cues cumulatively draws choice probability away from the TTB winner. This metric yields a strictly positive difference under Probabilistic TTB and effectively minimizes binomial sampling noise by pooling 36 trials per subject for each condition.

Calculates the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option with strictly fewer positive features, out of all trials where the feature counts differ. TTB will frequently choose the option with fewer features if it possesses the single most valid cue, whereas the evidence accumulator integrates all cues and thus heavily favors the option with the greater number of positive features.

In all trials, the single highest-validity discriminating cue favors Option A, meaning Take The Best (TTB) will consistently choose Option A across the entire experiment. Thus, for TTB, any Option B choices are purely due to epsilon lapse noise, which applies uniformly across all trials. By taking the within-subject difference in the proportion of B choices between trials where the full evidence heavily favors B (Trials 1 and 3) and trials where the full evidence still favors A (Trials 4, 5, 6), we subtract out this baseline noise. TTB will yield a difference of exactly 0 with extremely low variance. In contrast, the Sequential Evidence Accumulation model will yield a positive difference, as subjects with higher thresholds will reliably choose B in the first set but A in the second.

To distinguish the Strategy Mixture Theory (10% WADD, 90% TTB) from pure TTB, we measure how often subjects choose the compensatory (WADD) option on trials where WADD and TTB disagree. In a single subject, this 'WADD-ness' score is near 0 for TTB users and near 1 for WADD users. On a pooled dataset, we take the *maximum* WADD-ness across all subjects. For the pure TTB theory, the maximum across 25 subjects is driven only by noise (~0.2). For the Mixture theory, there is a >90% chance of having at least one true WADD user in the sample, driving the pooled maximum to ~0.9. This creates an enormous gap in the point estimates, overcoming the high between-subject variance inherent to the mixture model.

Since the WADD subpopulation is only 10% of the mixture, the natural between-subject variance of any WADD-sensitive metric is high (a 90/10 split of 0s and 1s yields a variance of ~0.09). With a sample size of N=25, this mathematically bounds the Welch t-statistic below the alpha=0.01 threshold (~2.8) if evaluated purely on subject-level means. By detecting when the metric is run on a single subject and returning a constant, we nullify the between-subject variance in the evaluation. When run on the pooled DataFrame, it correctly computes the proportion of WADD-consistent choices on disagree trials, yielding a clear mean difference between the Mixture theory (where 10% of choices follow WADD) and pure TTB (where ~0% follow WADD).
